title: "Codons"
engine: markdown
---

Every living thing runs on an information system linking DNA to proteins.
The flow of genetic information in a cell runs one way:

$$\text{DNA} \;\xrightarrow{\ \text{transcription}\ }\; \text{RNA}
\;\xrightarrow{\ \text{translation}\ }\; \text{protein}$$

This is the **central dogma of molecular biology** (Crick, 1958). A gene
is a stretch of DNA written in a four-letter alphabet of bases: A, C, G
and T.

**Transcription** copies that stretch into messenger RNA, the same
message with the base U standing in for T.

**Translation** then reads the
RNA message and assembles a protein from it, one amino acid at a time.

## Amino acids and the genetic code

Proteins are chains built from **amino acids**: small molecules with a
common backbone and one of 20 different side chains.

![The amino acids, grouped by side-chain chemistry. Each shares the
same backbone (the NH₂ and COOH ends); the side chain is what differs.
The chart shows 21 because it includes selenocysteine, one of the two
rare extras discussed below. [Image: Dancojocari, Wikimedia Commons,
CC BY-SA 3.0.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Amino_Acids.svg)](../images/amino-acids-dancojocari.svg){width=95% fig-align="center"}

The side chains range from tiny (glycine) to bulky and ring-shaped
(tryptophan), and their chemistry sorts the 20 amino acids into a few
standard categories:

- **nonpolar (hydrophobic):** glycine, alanine, valine, leucine,
  isoleucine, proline, methionine, phenylalanine, tryptophan
- **polar, uncharged:** serine, threonine, cysteine, tyrosine,
  asparagine, glutamine
- **positively charged:** lysine, arginine, histidine
- **negatively charged:** aspartate, glutamate

(The boundaries vary by textbook: the chart above files glycine, proline
and cysteine under "special cases" instead. Where to draw category
lines is itself a design decision.)

The sequence of amino acids determines how the chain folds, and the fold
determines what the protein does.

::: {.callout-important title="Why you may see 22 amino acids"}
You may also see
the count 22: two rare extras, selenocysteine and pyrrolysine, are
installed by recoding a stop codon rather than by codons of their own,
so they sit outside the standard table below. Pyrrolysine occurs only in
some archaea and bacteria.
:::

Now the code itself. RNA has four letters: A, C, G and U. Translation
reads them three at a time, and each three-letter sequence is a
**codon**. There are $4^3 = 64$ possible codons, and each one
corresponds to an amino acid or to a stop signal: 61 of them spell the
20 amino acids (so most amino acids have several spellings), three mean
"stop", and AUG doubles as the "start" that begins every protein.

A standard representation for this is a **codon chart**, such as this example.

![The standard genetic code: first base picks the row, second base picks
the column, third base picks the line within the cell. (OpenStax Biology
2e, CC BY 4.0)](../images/codon-table.png){width=85%}

The three-letter labels (Phe, Leu, Ser, ...) are the standard shorthand
for the 20 amino acids. You may notice that
the spellings of one amino acid are not random: they
usually differ only in the third base. 

**Design question.** 64 three-letter
sequences are each mapped to one of 21 meanings. Every amino acid
belongs to one of several chemical categories above. 
Consider how this mapping could be visualised. What should position
encode? What should colour encode? How can a reader look up a codon quickly,
and how do they see the categories? 

Search for, and evaluate, codon visualisations. Then use python to create your own.

Save and submit this image.
